    CHAPTER 10

    Discipline and Conduct

    "Talent might make you good but it’s your attitude and work ethic that will make you great."
    Purpose
    • Maintain a professional, respectful and safe working environment
    • To ensure that disciplinary action is consistent, fair and documented
    Benefit to Dealer
    • Clear conduct framework protects from legal and reputational risk
    • Disciplinary processes reduce the chance of wrongful claims
    • A culture of accountability improves overall discipline and reduces conflict
    Benefit to Customers
    • Customers interact with staff who represent the dealership's values
    • Better protection of personal and financial information

    Principles

    1. 01

      Conduct standards apply equally across all levels

    2. 02

      Every employee entitled to be heard before any action is taken

    3. 03

      The disciplinary process escalates progressively

    This chapter outlines the code of conduct expected from the employees.

    10.1 Code of Conduct

    The following code of Conduct applies to all dealerships and its employees and sets out the ethical requirements that are mandatory. If something feels wrong or inappropriate - even if it's not specifically written here - trust that instinct and think before you act.

    1. Professional Conduct & Appearance

    • Come to work on time
    • Wear proper uniform
    • Keep yourself well-groomed
    • Keep your work area clean and organized
    • Avoid using mobile phones for personal calls or social media when customers are around

    2. Customer Service Standards

    • Treat every customer with respect and patience
    • Listen carefully and give them your full attention
    • Never make false promises about repair completion times, service costs, or the work required on the vehicle

    3. Transparency & Business Practices

    • Always give complete and accurate information about:
      • Labour and parts charges
      • Work to be carried out and parts to be replaced
    • No hidden charges or surprises at delivery time
    • Only sell or fit authorized accessories and spare parts
    • Give written estimates before doing any additional work and get customer approval

    4. Data Privacy & Confidentiality

    • Keep all customer documents (Aadhar cards, PANs, RC, insurance policies, addresses) secure
    • Never share customer details outside the dealership
    • Don't discuss customer's:
      • Vehicle service history and repair details
      • Billing and insurance claim information
      • Personal matters with other customers or on social media

    5. Workplace Respect & Equal Treatment

    • Treat all colleagues with dignity regardless of their designation, gender, religion, caste, or background - no bullying, no inappropriate jokes, no harassment of any kind
    • If you face or witness any misbehaviour, discrimination, or harassment at work, report it immediately to HR or your manager

    6. Health & Safety

    • Follow all safety rules in the workshop - wear proper safety gear, handle tools correctly and never take shortcuts that could cause accidents
    • Report any unsafe conditions immediately (broken equipment, oil spills, electrical issues, expired fire extinguishers) before someone gets hurt

    7. Financial Integrity & Anti-Corruption

    • Never accept or give bribes, cash gifts, or kickbacks to/from customers, vendors, insurance surveyors, or insurance company staff
    • Don't take money from the cash counter, claim false expenses, or manipulate bills and invoices for personal benefit

    8. Legal & Regulatory Compliance

    • Follow all traffic rules during road tests, pick-up and drop, and vehicle movements; ensure all dealership vehicles (courtesy, pick-up and service vehicles) have valid insurance, pollution certificates and proper documentation
    • Don't help customers submit fake documents for insurance or warranty claims and don't use fake/duplicate parts - these are criminal offenses

    9. Conflict of Interest

    • If you have family members or personal business relationships with vendors or customers, inform your manager immediately
    • Don't do side businesses or part-time work that competes with the dealership, or use company time and resources for personal work

    10. Reporting Concerns & Whistleblower Protection

    • If you see theft, fraud, customer cheating, safety violations, or any wrong behaviour, speak up - report it to your manager, HR, or use anonymous email / written letter
    • You will not face any punishment, salary cuts, or bad treatment for honestly reporting genuine concerns; the company protects people who do the right thing

    10.2 Serious Misconduct Leading to Immediate Termination

    Money and property theft

    • Taking cash from the counter, fuel from vehicles, spare parts from stock, or any dealership property for personal use - even small amounts, even if you planned to "return it later"
    • Stealing anything that belongs to a customer - money, documents, belongings left in their vehicle during service

    Financial dishonesty with customers

    • Asking a customer to pay into your personal bank account, UPI, or giving them your personal account details instead of the dealership's official payment method
    • Keeping a portion of the customer's payment for yourself without the dealership's knowledge

    Taking illegal benefits from vendors

    • Accepting money, commissions, gifts, or any favours from insurance companies, insurance surveyors, part suppliers, or outside workshops in exchange for giving them business
    • Giving company business to a vendor because they're paying you personally, not because they're the best choice

    Faking business records

    • Creating fake job cards or repair orders for work that was never actually done, inflating labour hours or parts usage, or inflating numbers to meet targets
    • Changing, hiding, or lying about any official record - sales data, service reports, attendance, stock registers, or customer complaints

    Document forgery

    • Signing a customer's name on any document without their knowledge or permission - job cards, estimate approvals, vehicle delivery documents, anything
    • Creating fake documents like job cards, invoices, or insurance claim papers for customers or for yourself

    Misusing customer information

    • Selling customer contact lists, addresses, or financial details to other businesses, marketing companies, or individuals
    • Sharing confidential customer data outside the dealership for any reason other than official business purposes

    Lying during hiring

    • Giving false information in your job application or interview - fake degrees, inflated previous salary, hiding that you were terminated from your last job, or providing a fake experience certificate
    • Using someone else's documents or qualifications to get hired

    Sexual harassment

    • Making unwanted physical contact, sexual comments, inappropriate messages, or requests for sexual favours from any colleague or customer
    • Showing obscene material, making lewd gestures, or creating a hostile environment for anyone based on their gender (details covered separately in Section 10.3)

    Threatening or violent behaviour

    • Using abusive or threatening language toward customers, colleagues, or managers
    • Physical violence of any kind - pushing, hitting, threatening to harm someone, or destroying things in anger

    Coming to work intoxicated

    • Reporting to work under the influence of alcohol, drugs, or any substance that impairs your ability to work safely and professionally
    • Consuming alcohol or drugs during work hours, including lunch breaks

    Dangerous or illegal driving

    • Driving any dealership vehicle or customer vehicle without a valid driving license
    • Rash driving, over speeding, racing, or doing stunts with dealership or customer vehicles - especially during road tests and pick-up and drop, when the customer's vehicle is your responsibility

    Deliberately damaging property

    • Intentionally breaking, scratching, or vandalizing dealership property - vehicles, equipment, computers, workshop tools and lifts
    • Damaging a customer's vehicle deliberately during service or road test

    Unexplained long absence

    • Disappearing from work for several days without informing anyone - no call, no message, no explanation - leaving your team and customers stranded

    Working for a competitor or dual employment

    • Taking another full-time or part-time job with a competing dealership, brand, or automotive business while employed here
    • Running your own competing business (like vehicle reselling, spare parts shop) while working for the dealership without disclosure and approval

    Deliberate insubordination

    • Openly refusing to follow a clear, reasonable and legal instruction from your manager or supervisor
    • Repeatedly and intentionally ignoring direct orders that are part of your job responsibilities

    Criminal activity or actions harming JSW Motors reputation

    • Being involved in any illegal activity that becomes known publicly and damages the JSW Motors brand image
    • Any behaviour - on duty or off duty - that gets reported in news or social media and brings disrepute to the company

    Sabotage or espionage

    • Deliberately sabotaging dealership operations, passing confidential business information to competitors, or helping competitors harm the business

    Tampering with safety equipment

    • Disabling, removing, or tampering with safety devices, fire extinguishers, CCTV cameras, or security systems

    Fraudulent warranty or insurance claims

    • Filing fake warranty claims with JSW Motors or false insurance claims to benefit personally or help a customer fraudulently

    Bringing weapons to workplace

    • Carrying firearms, knives, or any weapons onto dealership premises (unless legally authorized security personnel)

    Allowing unauthorized people to work

    • Letting friends, family, or unauthorized people handle dealership operations, use dealership systems, or access restricted areas in your place

    10.3 The Disciplinary Process

    The process below is a step-by-step guide to handle any disciplinary issue allowing fairness and transparency in the approach ensuring all decisions are based on facts.

    Step #What HappensWhen
    Step 1: Verbal Counselling
    • The manager has a one-on-one conversation with the employee
    • It's informal but serious
    • They'll explain what went wrong, why it matters and what needs to change
    • This is documented in the manager's notes but doesn't go into employee’s official file yet
    		For first-time minor issues like occasional lateness, dress code violations, minor customer service lapses, or small procedural mistakes
    Step 2: Written Warning (First)
    • A warning email 10B is sent clearly stating what rule was broken, what the consequence was and what's expected going forward
    • This will be signed for acknowledging it was received (signing doesn't mean you agree, just that you saw it)
    • This goes into employee’s personnel file
    		When the verbal counselling didn't work and the behaviour repeated, OR for more serious issues like repeated tardiness, unauthorized absence, poor performance after coaching, or not following standard procedures / code of conduct
    Step 3: Written Warning (Final)
    • A second and final written warning using 10B
    • This one clearly states that if the behaviour happens again, employment will be terminated
    • It's the last chance
    • This also goes into employee's file and may affect increment or promotion eligibility
    		When the first written warning didn't result in improvement and the issue happened again, OR for serious misconduct like insubordination, significant policy violations, or behaviour that risks customer relationships or safety
    Step 4: Suspension Pending Investigation
    • Employee is asked to stay home (with or without pay, depending on the situation) while the dealership investigates a serious allegation
    • Employee will be sent a 10C suspension email explaining why
    • During this time, employee cannot come to the premises or contact customers/colleagues about work matters
    		When there's a serious allegation that needs thorough investigation—like theft, fraud, harassment, violence, or major safety violations—and it's better for everyone if you're not at work while facts are gathered
    Step 5: Show Cause Notice & Inquiry
    • A formal "show cause notice" listing the allegations against you and asking employee to explain his / her side in writing within a set timeframe (usually 48-72 hours)
    • If needed, a formal inquiry meeting is held where employee can present their version, bring witnesses, or have a colleague accompany them for support
    • Management reviews all evidence before coming to a decision
    		For serious or gross misconduct, or when earlier steps haven't worked and termination is being considered. This ensures you get a fair hearing and the dealership has proper documentation before making a final decision
    Step 6: Termination of Employment
    • After completing the inquiry and reviewing employee’s response, if the evidence supports that employee committed serious misconduct or didn't improve despite multiple warnings, employment is terminated
    • A termination letter is issued stating the reasons, final settlement details and last working day
    		When all previous steps have been exhausted without improvement, OR immediately for gross misconduct offenses listed in the immediate termination section (theft, fraud, violence, etc.)

    The enquiry flow

    If an employee does not attend the enquiry despite receiving proper notice, the enquiry may proceed in their absence. All notices issued and records of non-attendance should be documented and retained.

    Things to be careful about

    • Do not decide the outcome before completing the enquiry
    • Maintain proper records of all documents, including notices, responses, investigation records, findings and final decisions
    • Do not discuss the matter around the dealership
    • Do not let a manager handle a case where they are personally involved
    • Apply the same standard to everybody regardless of the position or seniority
    • If a criminal offence has taken place, such as theft, the dealership may also file a police complaint. The internal process still must be followed

    Appeal

    If an employee believes a disciplinary decision is unfair, they may submit a written appeal to the HR Manager or Dealer Principal within seven days. The appeal will be reviewed and a final decision will be shared in writing within fifteen days.

    10.4 POSH: Prevention of Sexual Harassment

    This is governed by the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013.

    What counts as sexual harassment

    Any unwelcome behaviour of a sexual nature. This includes:

    • Physical contact or advances
    • Asking for or demanding sexual favours
    • Sexually coloured remarks, jokes or comments about a person's body
    • Showing pornography
    • Any other unwelcome physical, verbal or non-verbal conduct of a sexual nature, including messages, photographs and social media

    The workplace includes the workshop, the service reception, the parts store, the parking area, a customer's home during a pick-up, drop or doorstep service visit, a road test, an event, an outing and a work trip. It also covers work-related messages and calls outside office hours.

    The internal committee

    Every dealership with ten or more employees must have an Internal Committee also called as IC. This is a legal requirement, not a recommendation.

    PositionWho
    Presiding OfficerA senior woman employee of the dealership
    MembersAt least two employees committed to the cause of women, or with experience in social work or law
    External MemberOne member from an NGO or a person familiar with issues relating to sexual harassment. Not an employee of the dealership
    CompositionAt least half of the members must be women
    TermThree years

    Where the dealership has no senior woman employee, the Presiding Officer may be nominated from another outlet of the same dealer partner.

    How a complaint is handled

    StepWhat happensTime
    1The complaint is made in writing to the IC using annexure 10E. If the woman cannot write it herself, the IC must help her put it in writing.Within 3 months of the incident, extendable by 3 months
    2The IC may first offer conciliation, if the woman asks for it. No money settlement is allowed as the basis of conciliation.Before the enquiry
    3The IC holds an enquiry. Both sides are heard. Confidentiality is maintained throughout.Completed within 90 days
    4The IC gives its report to the Dealer Principal.Within 10 days of completing the enquiry
    5The Dealer Principal acts on the recommendation.Within 60 days of the report
    6Either side may appeal.Within 90 days

    While the enquiry is going on

    • The person may ask for a transfer, for the other person to be transferred, or for leave of up to three months. This leave is in addition to her normal leave.
    • The identity of everybody involved is kept confidential. Discussing the case around the dealership is itself a disciplinary matter.
    • No action of any kind may be taken against the woman for having complained. Any pressure or unfair treatment after a complaint is major misconduct.

    What the dealership must do

    • Display the names and contact details of the IC members where everybody can see them
    • Explain POSH to every new joiner during induction, including men
    • Run an awareness session at least once a year through certified POSH trainer
    • Train the IC members through certified POSH trainer
    • File the annual return with the District Officer
    • Include a POSH section in every appointment letter and the conduct code

    A knowingly false complaint made to harm somebody is also a disciplinary matter.

    10.5 Grievance Handling

    A grievance is any work-related problem, concern, or complaint that's bothering an employee’s and affecting their job, dignity, or workplace experience. The steps taken to resolve the grievance is also beneficial to ensure a healthy workplace environment.

    Grievance Resolution Steps

    Step #ActivityWho Is InvolvedTimeline
    Step 1: Informal Resolution
    • Talk directly to immediate supervisor or manager about the issue
    • Most problems can be solved quickly through an honest conversation
    • Explanation about what happened, what's bothering the employee and what would fix it
    		Employee + Immediate Manager/SupervisorWithin 2-3 days of the issue occurring
    Step 2: Formal Written Grievance
    • If talking to manager didn't help, or if the issue involves employee’s manager, submit a written grievance to HR (annexure 10F)
    • Write down what happened (with dates and details), who was involved and what is to be done about it
    • One can submit it in person, by email, or through the grievance box if available
    		Employee submits to HR Manager/Dealership HeadWithin 7 days of Step 1, or immediately if Step 1 isn't possible
    Step 3: Acknowledgment & Initial Review
    • HR or management acknowledges that they've received the complaint and gives a reference number
    • They do a quick review to understand the issue and decide how serious it is and who should investigate
    		HR Manager reviews and assigns investigationWithin 2 working days of receiving the grievance
    Step 4: Investigation
    • HR or an assigned manager investigates by talking to the concerned party, talking to the person complained about (if applicable), interviewing witnesses and reviewing any documents or evidence
    • Everything is kept as confidential as possible
    		HR/Investigating Officer + Employee + Relevant partiesWithin 7-10 working days from acknowledgment
    Step 5: Resolution & Communication
    • Based on the investigation, management decides what action to take - this could be counselling someone, changing a policy, taking disciplinary action, or explaining why no action is needed
    • You receive a written response explaining what was found and what will be done
    		HR/Management communicates decision to employeeWithin 3-5 working days after investigation is complete
    Step 6: Appeal (if not satisfied)
    • If not satisfied with the resolution or feel the investigation wasn't fair, an appeal can be made to a higher authority - the dealership owner, regional HR head, or the JSW Motors grievance channel
    • The appeal must be put in writing explaining why the decision was wrong
    		Employee appeals to Higher Management/JSW Motors Escalation ChannelWithin 7 days of receiving the Step 5 resolution
    Step 7: Final Review & Closure
    • The higher authority reviews everything, the original complaint, investigation findings, appeal and any new information
    • A final decision is made which is communicated to relevant parties in writing. This decision is final
    		Senior Management/JSW Motors TeamWithin 10-15 working days from receiving the appeal

    Important Points to Remember

    • Every grievance is taken seriously – Raising a genuine grievance through proper channels will not result in any punishment, transfer, salary cut, or bad treatment. If anyone retaliates against anyone for complaining, that itself is a serious violation.
    • Confidentiality is maintained – The complaint is handled discreetly. Only people who need to know (to investigate or resolve it) will be informed.
    • False complaints have consequences – If investigation proves employee deliberately made a false complaint to harm someone or create trouble, the said employee may face disciplinary action yourself. But this only applies to intentionally false complaints, not genuine concerns that turned out to be misunderstandings.
    • Emergency issues – For serious matters like harassment, violence, theft, or safety emergencies report immediately to HR, the dealership head, or reach out to the JSW Motors team.
    • Anonymous reporting option – Employee can use anonymous email to report serious violations without revealing their identity, though it may limit how thoroughly the issue can be investigated.
    • Keep records – Save copies of written grievance, any emails and the responses. If things get complicated later, these will be proofs of what was said and when.

    Grievance committee

    If required by law, the dealership must establish a Grievance Committee with representatives from both employees and management. The committee should also include adequate representation of women. HR is responsible for monitoring legal requirements and ensuring the committee is formed in a timely manner.

    CHAPTER 11

    Employee Exit Management

    "Resignation should not turn an employee into an enemy. Every employee deserves a respectful exit."
    Purpose
    • To ensure employee exits are handled professionally and fairly
    • Apply appropriate insights to improve the overall employee experience
    Benefit to Dealer
    • Proper handover process protects dealership operations and customer relationships
    • Reason of exit helps retention improvement initiatives
    • Safeguards dealership from legal and compliance risk
    Benefit to Customers
    • Maintain continuity of customer relationships through handover

    Principles

    1. 01

      Exit managed through a defined process and approval

    2. 02

      Fully documented and recorded exit with confidentiality

    3. 03

      Full and final settlement completed within a defined timeline

    In this chapter, we will understand a standard exit management process that must be followed across all JSW Motors dealerships.

    11.1 Exit Process

    1

    Resignation by employee or dealership takes termination decision

    Employee/ HR Manager
    2

    One-on-one meeting with the employee

    Reporting Manager + HR Manager
    3

    Decide if the employee is to be retained or not

    Reporting Manager + HR Manager
    4

    Resignation acceptance email shared

    HR Manager
    5

    Handover list prepared

    Employee with Reporting Manager
    6

    Role handover completed

    Employee and successor/ Manager
    7

    Conduct exit interview 3 days before the last working day.

    HR Manager
    8

    Clearance form completed with all assets handed over.

    HR Manager/Accounts
    9

    Full and final settlement, relieving letter and experience letter shared

    HR and Accounts

    11.1.1 Resignation by employee or dealership takes termination decision

    • Employee shares resignation email to reporting and HR Manager
    • Dealership takes termination decision due to conduct or performance issues

    11.1.2 One-on-one meeting with the employee

    • On resignation day, reporting manager arranges a one-on-one meeting with the employee
    • HR Manager also arranges a one-on-one meeting with the employee to understand any concerns

    11.1.3 Decide if the employee is to be retained or not

    • Reporting and HR Manager together decide if the employee is to be retained

    11.1.4 Resignation acceptance email shared

    • HR Manager must provide acceptance on the resignation email within 3 working days using annexure 11A
    • Last working day as per the notice period must be mentioned in the email:
    StageNotice Period
    During probation15 days
    After confirmation, Customer Facing and Support roles30 days
    After confirmation, Leadership roles60 days
    • Notice can be shortened by mutual agreement in writing
    • Notice can be bought out by the employee or next employer or waived off by the dealership
    • Leaves cannot be taken during notice period. For emergencies, manager approval is required for leaves

    11.1.5 Handover list prepared

    • The handover should include the transfer of:
      • -key responsibilities
      • -ongoing tasks
      • -critical contacts
      • -important documentation
    • Knowledge transfer sessions should be conducted by the reporting manager with the receiving employee
    • Return or transfer ownership of company assets
    • The resigned employee and the employee taking handover signs the annexure 11B
    • System access is removed on the last working day

    11.1.6 Role handover completed

    • Handover of all roles and responsibilities must be completed 5 days before the last working day

    11.1.7 Conduct exit interview

    An exit interview gives an opportunity to share feedback on overall employment experience

    It is to be done by the HR Manager 3 days before the last working day around the following lines:

    • Reason for leaving
    • About the role & manager in terms of expectations, support & guidance
    • About the work environment
    • About the growth & development
    • About compensation and benefits
    • Preference for come back and recommendation to friends & colleagues
    • Open feedback

    Use annexure 11C to capture exit interview response.

    HR should read all the exit interviews forms and share the findings with the Dealer Principal.

    11.1.8 Clearance form completed

    • All assets like laptop, sim card, etc. must be handed over to the HR Manager before exit
    • Post handover of assets, annexure 11B will be completed by the HR Manager, Accounts and Business Head
    • If the employee is joining another JSW Motors dealership, the HR Manager issues an NOC or clearance certificate once the 11B clearance is complete (the new dealership needs it before joining; see 3.1.10)
    • The NOC is not withheld once the handover is complete and dues are settled. It is issued within 3 working days of clearance

    11.1.9 Full and final settlement done

    • Salary dues must be settled within 2 days of last working day
    • Gratuity, where payable, is released with F&F settlement
    • Provident Fund is claimed by the employee and HR can help with the paperwork
    • Earned incentive for tenure completed months is paid as part of full and final settlement
    • Any advance or dues are adjusted
    • The relieving and experience letter (annexure 11D) are given as soon as the settlement is done

    11.2 Manpower Attrition

    • Employee exiting the dealership after 60 days of employment, are considered for attrition monitoring
    • The roles to be considered for calculating manpower attrition are:
      • Service Advisor
      • Technician
      • Job Controller
      • CRE/M
    • Manpower attrition is calculated on a monthly rolling basis (last 12 months)
    • The HR Manager needs to find out the reason for attrition during exit interview and share it with management for improvement
    • Use the below formula to calculate manpower attrition rate:
    Manpower Attrition=Manpower Left / (Manpower Opening + Manpower Joined) x 100

    Note: (Manpower >60 days old)

    Example: ABC Automobiles | Attrition Calculation | Dec 2025
    • Total Service Advisors, Technicians and Job Controllers, CRE Left (Jan 25 – Dec 25) = 36
    • Total Manpower Joined (Jan 25 – Dec 25) = 40
    • Opening Manpower (1st Dec 25) = 68
    • Attrition Dec 2025 = [ 36 / ( 40 + 68 ) ] X 100 = 33%

    "Always treat your employees exactly as you want them to treat your best customers."
    Purpose

    • Statutory compliance protects from penalties and litigation

    Principles

    1. 01

    This chapter covers all the policies that are necessary for dealership operations.

    12.1 Working Hours, Attendance and Week-off Policy

    Purpose:

    • To set standard working hours, attendance, late coming and week off arrangements
    • Ensure the dealership operates consistently and every employee knows what is expected

    Scope: Applies to all employees across all functions and outlets of the dealership

    Working hours

    ItemRecommended
    Working hours9 hours a day including the break and not more than 54 hours in a week
    Workshop timing9:30 am to 7:00 pm (or any other work shift assigned by the manager)
    Lunch break45 minutes
    Week offOne full day every week, on rotation. Usually, a weekday for service advisors and technicians, because Saturdays (and Sundays where the workshop is open) are peak days
    Working on the week offCompensatory off within 30 days, or overtime pay as per law
    OvertimePaid at twice the ordinary rate OR as the law requires. It must be recorded

    Roster

    • The manager maintains the roster on DMS considering the shifts required to run the dealership operations.
    • Week offs rotate. The same person should not always get Monday while somebody else always gets a good day.
    • Workshop coverage comes first. The roster must always leave enough service advisors and technicians on the floor on peak days, especially weekends.
    • If the weekly off is changed at short notice, the person is told the reason and given another day off that week.
    • During a festival period or a big campaign, week offs may be adjusted. Tell people in advance, not on the day.

    Marking attendance

    • Use biometric system only.
    • Attendance is marked when arriving and when leaving.
    • Nobody marks attendance for somebody else.
    • For staff who go out for pick-up and drop, roadside assistance, doorstep service, he/she should send a note to the reporting manager/HR, so they are not shown absent.

    Attendance records

    • Leave record must be updated.
    • HR closes attendance for the month by the date fixed for payroll, usually the 25th.
    • Any correction must be requested before the closing date. After payroll is processed, it is adjusted the subsequent month.
    • Records are kept as the law requires and may be kept in electronic form.

    If you cannot come to work

    • Inform the reporting manager before the shift starts.
    • Then apply for leave in the system on the same day or the next working day.
    • Absent without informing your manager is treated as leave without pay and repeated cases are a disciplinary matter.
    • Absent for a period more than 5 working days without information is absconding which may lead to legal proceedings.

    Late coming

    SituationWhat happens
    Up to 15 minutes lateAllowed two days a month
    Late three times in a monthThe manager has a word
    Late more than three times in a monthHalf day leave deducted for each further late mark
    Habitually lateWritten warning from HR Manager

    Women working at night

    Women may work after dark, but only if they agree to it and only if the dealership makes proper arrangements:

    • safe transport from the dealership to home
    • adequate lighting
    • security on the premises
    • never a woman working alone

    This is now also a legal requirement in many states.

    Late sitting

    • If people are kept back, arrange food and transport
    • Late sitting should be the exception and approved by reporting manager

    Disclaimer: HR to follow territory and state labour laws.

    12.2 Leaves and Holiday Policy

    Purpose:

    • To give every employee a clear entitlement to all types of leaves and holidays
    • Defined process for leave application and approval

    Scope: Applies to all full-time employees of the dealership

    TypeHow many daysFor what
    Earned Leave12 days a yearPlanned leave, holidays, personal work. Applied for in advance
    Casual Leave5 days a yearShort, unplanned needs. Usually, one or two days at a time
    Sick Leave5 days a yearIllness. Medical certificate needed if more than 2 days together
    Maternity Leave26 weeksFor the first two children. 12 weeks for the third onwards, as per law
    Paternity Leave7 daysRecommended, not required by law. To be taken within one month of the birth
    Bereavement Leave3 daysDeath of a close family member
    Marriage Leave3 daysOwn marriage. Once during service
    Compensatory OffAs earnedFor working on a week off or a holiday. To be used within 30 days
    Leave Without PayAs approvedWhen no other leave is left. Approved by the Dealer Principal

    Applying for leave

    Type of leaveHow much notice
    Earned leave, 1 to 3 daysAt least 3 days before
    Earned leave, more than 3 daysAt least 15 days before
    Casual leaveAt least 1 day before, or the same morning in an emergency
    Sick leaveInform the manager before the shift. Apply on return
    Maternity leaveAt least 8 weeks before

    Approving leave

    • The reporting manager approves. HR records it
    • Answer within two working days
    • Leave can be refused only for a genuine business reason and the reason must be explained
    • If leave is refused, offer another set of dates
    • Not more than two people from a small team should be on leave at the same time, unless the manager agrees
    • Before going on leave, the person hands over their work in progress jobs to a named colleague

    Other leave FAQs

    QuestionAnswer
    Can earned leave be carried forward?Yes. Up to 24 days. Anything above is encashed or lapses as per the state rule
    Can leave be encashed?Earned leave only, at the time of leaving and once a year if the dealership allows it
    Do casual and sick leave carry forward?No. They lapse at the end of the year
    Can casual leave be joined with earned leave?No. Casual leave is for short, unplanned needs
    Is a holiday inside a long leave counted?A holiday or week off falling in the middle of earned leave is counted as leave
    Leave during notice period?Only with the manager’s written agreement
    Leave during probation?Casual and sick leave yes, in proportion. Earned leave is normally taken after confirmation

    Holidays

    • The dealership publishes its holiday list for the year before the year starts
    • National holidays must be given: 26 January, 15 August and 2 October
    • Other holidays are chosen based on the local festivals in that town
    • Around 10 holidays in the year are normal
    • The workshop may stay open on a festival day to meet customer demand for servicing or vehicle delivery. Staff who work get compensatory off or holiday pay as per law

    Disclaimer: HR to follow territory and state labour laws

    Local travel

    Travel within the dealership city limits

    How they travelWhat is paidRecommended
    Own two-wheelerPer kilometre₹ xx per km
    Own carPer kilometre₹ xx per km

    How to claim

    • Get written approval before travelling. An email or a signed travel form is enough.
    • Take a travel advance if needed. Ask HR at least two days before.
    • Keep the tickets and bills. A claim without a bill is settled only at the Business Head’s discretion.

    • Personal travel added to a business trip is at the employee’s own cost.

    CHAPTER 13

    Leadership Practices

    "Before you are a leader, success is all about growing yourself. When you become a leader, success is all about growing others." – Jack Welch
    Objective
    • :
    • Make sure no critical aftersales role is left without a capable person

    Benefit to Dealer
    • Business continuity when a key person resigns, is promoted or is on long leave

    Principles

    1. 01

    2. 02

    3. 03

    This chapter covers three Leader-level practices: succession planning, communication and leadership development.

    13.1 Succession Planning

    Succession planning means naming and preparing at least one successor for every critical role before the role falls vacant.

    13.1.1 Critical roles

    The following aftersales roles are critical. The Dealer Principal may add others.

    Critical roleTarget no. of successors [confirm]Typical successor pool
    General Manager – Service2Service Manager, Bodyshop Manager
    Service Manager2Workshop Controller, Senior Service Advisor
    Bodyshop Manager1Bodyshop Controller, Bodyshop SA
    Parts Manager1Parts Executive
    CRM Service1Senior CRE Service, Service Reception Co-ordinator
    Workshop Controller1Master Technician (L3), Senior Service Advisor, Quality Controller
    Diagnostic Expert1Senior Technician (L2), Electrical Expert
    Warranty Specialist1Service Advisor, Quality Controller
    Internal Dealer Trainer1Master Technician, Senior Service Advisor

    13.1.2 Succession planning process

    StepActivityWhoWhen
    1Confirm the critical-role list and flag roles at risk (incumbent likely to move, retire or leave within 12 months)HR Manager with GM – ServiceApril, after the annual appraisal (or as per appraisal cycle)
    2Place eligible employees on the talent grid (13.1.3) using the annual rating and manager input on potentialReporting Manager + HR ManagerApril
    3Nominate successors for each critical role and set their readiness level (13.1.4)GM – Service, approved by Dealer PrincipalBy 30 April
    4Agree an Individual Development Plan (IDP) for each successor using annexure 13BReporting Manager + successor + IDTBy 15 May
    5Review IDP progress and update readinessGM – Service + HR ManagerQuarterly, with the Chapter 7 reviews
    6Record the plan in annexure 13AHR ManagerAnnually, by 31 May

    The succession plan is confidential. Successors are told they are in a development programme, not that they have been promised a role.

    13.1.3 Talent grid

    Performance comes from the latest Chapter 7 rating. Potential is judged by the reporting manager and GM – Service on learning agility, ownership, people skills and acceptance by the team.

    Potential ↓ / Performance →Rating 1–2Rating 3Rating 4–5
    HighCoach, re-check fitDevelop for next roleSuccessor – fast track
    MediumImprove in current roleCore contributorSuccessor – develop
    LowPIP (Chapter 7.2.4 [confirm ref])Retain in roleExpert in role

    Only employees in the "Successor – fast track", "Successor – develop" and "Develop for next role" cells are nominated as successors.

    13.1.4 Readiness levels

    LevelMeaningAction
    Ready nowCan take the role within 30 daysName as acting cover for leave or sudden exit
    Ready in 1–2 yearsMeets most Chapter 8 step-up criteria; gaps are knownIDP with stretch assignments and Chapter 13.3 programme
    Ready in 2+ yearsHigh potential, early in careerFocus on current-role mastery and certification

    Every critical role should have at least one successor who is Ready now or Ready in 1–2 years. [confirm target]

    13.1.5 Emergency cover

    • When a critical role falls vacant without notice, the Ready now successor acts in the role within 07 working days
    • The acting period lasts up to 90 days ; the role is then filled through the IJP process in Chapter 3.1.3
    • ”Acting” cover is not a promotion; the Chapter 8 promotion process still applies

    13.1.6 Best Practice

    • Give successors short stretch assignments: run the morning meeting, chair a mid-month review, or cover the role during the incumbent's leave
    • Track "bench strength" (% of critical roles with a ready successor) as an HR KPI on the monthly HR MIS
    • Keep the Chapter 3 backup pool for frontline roles and this succession plan for supervisory roles

    13.2 Communication

    Every employee should hear about business results, changes and decisions from their own manager, on a fixed schedule, and have a safe way to speak up.

    13.2.1 Communication cadence

    The meetings already set in Chapter 7.3 continue; this table adds the people-focused forums around them.

    ForumFrequencyLed byAttended byPurpose
    Morning meetingDaily, 15 min, before workshop openingService Manager / Bodyshop ManagerAll workshop, front-office and CRM staffDay's load, yesterday's results, one recognition, one safety or process point
    Mid-month reviewMonthly, by the 15thGM – ServiceDepartment headsKPI run-rate, corrective actions (Chapter 7.3)
    Monthly business reviewMonthlyDealer Principal / CEOGM – Service, department heads, HR ManagerResults, people metrics (attrition, training, vacancies)
    Town hallQuarterlyDealer PrincipalAll employeesDealership performance, JSW Motors updates, awards (Chapter 9), open Q&A
    Skip-level meetingQuarterlyGM – ServiceGroups of 8–10 frontline staff, without their direct managerHear concerns and ideas first-hand
    HR open houseMonthly, fixed day and hourHR ManagerAny employee, walk-inPolicy, pay, leave and personal queries
    Pulse surveyQuarterly, 5 questionsHR ManagerAll employees, anonymousEarly warning on morale and manager issues
    Employee satisfaction surveyAnnualHR ManagerAll employees, anonymousEngagement score by team; input to the Leadership Excellence Award (Chapter 9)

    The HR Manager publishes the year's communication calendar (annexure 13C) in December, together with the engagement calendar in Chapter 9.1

    13.2.2 What must be communicated, and how

    InformationChannelTiming
    Incentive scheme and targetsEmail + morning meeting (Chapter 4.4 )Before the period starts
    Policy changes (leave, attendance, uniform, travel)Email + notice board + morning meetingAt least 7 days before the change takes effect [confirm]
    Roster and week-off changesRoster in DMS + direct messageAs per Chapter 12.1
    New joiners, promotions, exitsEmail announcementOn the day
    JSW Motors circulars and product updatesLMS bulletin + morning meetingWithin 2 working days of receipt
    Awards and recognitionMorning meeting, town hall, notice board, social mediaAs per Chapter 9

    13.2.3 Two-way channels

    • Speak to your manager first – the default route for day-to-day concerns
    • Suggestion box / digital form – ideas on process, customer experience and safety; reviewed monthly by the GM – Service
    • Grievance process – as per Chapter 10.5
    • Whistleblower route – as per Chapter 10.1, for fraud, theft or safety concerns
    • Skip-level and pulse survey – for issues an employee will not raise with their own manager

    13.2.4 Close the loop

    • Every suggestion, common survey concern and skip-level issue gets a response within 30 days, even when the answer is no
    • Survey results are shared with all employees at the next town hall

    13.2.5 Best Practice

    • Hold morning meetings standing, at a fixed time and place, and end on time
    • Use the local language where most of the team is more comfortable in it
    • The HR Manager keeps a "You said, we did" board in the staff area and updates it monthly
    • Track communication as a KPI: % of scheduled forums held and pulse-survey participation

    13.3 Leadership Development

    Three programmes prepare employees to lead people. They correspond to the step-up requirements in Chapter 8. [confirm programme names match Chapter 8]

    13.3.1 Leadership programmes

    TierProgramme (name used in Chapter 8)ForComplete beforeCore modules
    1Supervisory Skills ProgrammeWorkshop Controller, Bodyshop Controller, Senior Service Advisor, Senior CRE, PDI In-charge, Washing Supervisor, and their successorsFirst supervisory roleFrom doer to supervisor; job allocation and daily planning; running a morning meeting; giving feedback; handling conflict on the floor; attendance, leave and discipline basics (Chapters 10, 12); safety leadership
    2Leadership Development ProgrammeService Manager, Bodyshop Manager, Parts Manager, CRM Service, and their successorsFirst manager roleSetting SMART KPIs and running reviews (Chapter 7); coaching and PIP; interviewing and selection (Chapter 3); engagement and retention; escalation handling; budgeting and cost control
    3Business Management & P&L ProgrammeGM – Service and successorsGM / Service Head roleAftersales P&L and business planning; building the succession plan (13.1); leading change; working with JSW Motors and partners; leading leaders

    Duration and delivery partner for each tier are to be set by JSW Motors

    13.3.2 How leaders learn (70:20:10)

    The programmes follow the same 70:20:10 rule as Chapter 6:

    • 70% on the job – taking on bigger tasks, standing in for a manager who is away (13.1.5), leading a real improvement project such as reducing repeat repairs or TAT
    • 20% from others – a named mentor one level up, fortnightly; peer learning with leaders from other JSW Motors dealerships
    • 10% formal – the Tier 1–3 sessions, LMS modules and certification

    13.3.3 Process

    StepActivityWhoWhen
    1Nominate participants from the succession plan and new role holdersGM – Service + HR ManagerMay, after 13.1
    2Training Needs Analysis (TNA): identify each participant's skill gaps using the manager rating, a short team feedback survey and the IDP, and agree the modules to focus onHR ManagerBefore the first session
    3Attend sessions and complete LMS modulesParticipantAs per JSW Motors calendar
    4Post-programme assessment and certificationHR Manager + IDTWithin 90 days of completion
    5Record completion in the training records (Chapter 6.7 ) and the IDPIDTWithin 2 days

    13.3.4 Measuring leaders

    In addition to their business KPIs, every people manager is reviewed annually on:

    • Team attrition (Chapter 11.2 formula )
    • Team engagement score from the annual satisfaction survey
    • Team training and certification completion (Chapter 6)
    • Bench strength: a ready successor named for their own role (13.1)
    • Forums held as scheduled (13.2.1)

    These are added to the manager's KPI form (annexure 7B ) with a suggested weight of 20%. [confirm]

    13.3.5 Best Practice

    • Promote only after the relevant tier is complete, in line with Chapter 8 eligibility criteria [confirm]
    • Invite a JSW Motors leader to speak at each programme
    • Rotate high-potential supervisors through Service, Bodyshop and CRM for short periods to build a whole-aftersales view
